narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth and fifth deciles among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a consistent pattern of academic struggle that strongly outweighed other information.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in your favor. At 3.20 it sits only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model a small reason to be more optimistic.

Your LSAT score of 35, middle-family income, and plan to attend full-time were less influential and did not change the overall outlook.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, or explore schools and programs with different admissions criteria that place less weight on early law-school performance. Reapplying with a clearer plan to address these academic gaps would be the most productive next step.
